chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shazan, all together from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Muawiya ibn 'Ammar, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Mudabbar (conditionally emancipated slave). He (peace be upon him) said: 'He is in the status of the bequest; the master may retract from him whatever he desires of the emancipation.'

key_terms.الْمُدَبَّر: Mudabbar: A slave whose emancipation is conditioned upon a specific event, typically the death of the master.
key_terms.الْوَصِيَّة: Al-Wasiyyah: The bequest or legacy, typically referring to the portion of estate given to non-heirs.
key_terms.يَرْجِعُ: Yarji'u: To retract, revoke, or return to a previous state.

ai.seo_question: What is the legal status of a Mudabbar in Shia fiqh and can the master revoke his emancipation?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the legal status of the 'Mudabbar' by equating it to a bequest (wasiyyah), granting the master discretionary power to revoke or fulfill the emancipation condition at will. This ruling highlights the flexibility in Shia jurisprudence regarding conditional manumission, distinguishing it from absolute ownership or fixed inheritance rights. The narration underscores the master's autonomy in managing this specific type of slave, reflecting broader principles of property disposition in Islamic law.
